blocks.text: That the dove was given the name יונה because it had been brought from Greece into Asia seems hardly probable. For what Bochart proves with a great display of learning, that doves are mentioned in Greece from all time past, is irrelevant to the matter. Does it follow from this that doves were native to no other region, or that they were brought from Greece into Asia? I am therefore surprised that this opinion pleased Michaelis, so much that he even adorned it with new arguments, in the Supplemm. ad Lexx. vol. 4, p. 1094 ff. I would think that the dove was given its name from its gentleness, a notion present in the Arabic verbs أَانَ [ʾāna] and هَانَ [hāna], whence أون [ʾawn] is mildness, affability, and هون [hawn] gentleness, mildness, so that it corresponds in a way to the Chaldee הון, rest, ease. Other conjectures on the reason for that name will be given by Simonis in the Arcanum Formarum, p. 42.

The emptiness of this opinion has been shown at length by J. D. Michaelis in the Supplemm. vol. 4, p. 1096 ff., and in the Observationes Criticae et Philologicae in Ieremiae Vaticinia, on Chapter XXV, 38., with which compare Schleusner, a most reverend man, on Michaelis' Observationes in Ierem. XLVI, 16, p. 309.
This interpretation has been defended by the two men praised in the preceding note, in the places mentioned there.
